newsitem.title: USA: People rely on friends' advice in choosing doctors.
newsitem.headline: People rely on friends' advice in choosing doctors.

text.p: Americans are more likely to rely on advice of family and friends when choosing a doctor or health plan than on recommendations from employers or independent rankings, a new study showed Monday.

The findings in a study by the nonprofit Kaiser Family Foundation and the U.S. government's Agency for Health Care Policy and Research came at a time when experts, businesses and think tanks were struggling to develop accurate "report cards" or other measures of health-care quality.

This field, known as quality research, has become more important as health care becomes more market-driven. As health plans compete on the basis of cost, consumers want assurances that quality is not being sacrificed.
Nearly six out of 10 people surveyed said they did not think their employers were a good source of information "because employers' main concern is saving money on health benefits."
Local news outlets' ratings also carried little weight, figuring in only 15 percent of the choices, the study found.

"For the health care market to work for people, they need a way to make choices based on quality. This study suggests we may still be a long way from that goal," said Kaiser foundation president Drew Altman.
Among the other findings, the survey found that people were more likely to stick to a hospital or doctor they were familiar with rather than one that got better ratings from an outside source.
At the same time, the survey found people did want reliable independent information, particularly about patient experiences and attitudes.
For instance, they wanted to know if patients had filed complaints against a doctor, about patient satisfaction and about how much preventive care a health plan offers.

Experts in health care quality study those trends but they also work on "outcome" research, in which they measure how patients with certain diseases or health problems fare in terms of recovery, complications or mortality.
The study was based on a telephone survey conducted by Princeton Survery Resarch Associates of 2,006 adults between July 26 and Sept. 5, 1996.
